questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of JSON logs over plain text?
options: You can query by field instead of matching text patterns
questions.explanation: Field based queries are reliable, while text matching breaks whenever a message changes.

questions.prompt: Why attach the service name and environment to every log line?
options: So logs from different sources can be told apart once combined
questions.explanation: Once several services log to one place, context is the only way to filter.

questions.prompt: What problem does a correlation identifier solve?
options: Following one run when several are writing to the same log
questions.explanation: Without it, interleaved lines from concurrent runs are impossible to separate.

questions.prompt: Where should the correlation identifier be generated?
options: Once at the start of the run, then passed through
questions.explanation: One identifier per run is the whole point, so it is created once.

questions.prompt: Why measure how long parts of your code take?
options: Because you cannot improve what you have not measured
questions.explanation: Guessing which part is slow is usually wrong, and measuring is cheap.

questions.prompt: Why wrap timing in a reusable helper?
options: So measuring any block costs one line instead of repeated boilerplate
questions.explanation: Instrumentation that is awkward to add does not get added.

questions.prompt: What does a metric dimension let you do?
options: Split one metric by a category such as environment
questions.explanation: It is the difference between one number and a number you can break down.

questions.prompt: What makes a good metric to track for a tool?
options: A small number that tell you whether it is working and how hard
questions.explanation: Too many metrics is the same problem as too many alerts.

questions.prompt: What should a health check return?
options: A clear status and an exit code reflecting it
questions.explanation: Something automated has to be able to act on the answer.

questions.prompt: Why break a dependency deliberately when testing a health check?
options: To confirm the check actually detects the problem
questions.explanation: An untested check is an assumption, exactly like an untested alarm.

questions.prompt: What connects structured logging here to your Month 3 bash work?
options: Both aim to produce output another tool can consume reliably
questions.explanation: Consistent, parseable output has been the theme since your first toolkit.

questions.prompt: Why does instrumentation matter for a tool you wrote yourself?
options: Because you will need to debug it when it fails unattended
questions.explanation: Your scheduled audit is exactly the kind of thing that fails quietly.

questions.prompt: Text matching on log messages is fragile because messages change.
questions.explanation: A field name is stable in a way a sentence in a log message is not.

questions.prompt: A correlation identifier is only useful in large distributed systems.
questions.explanation: Two concurrent runs of your own script produce the same interleaving problem.

questions.prompt: Measuring your code before optimising it is more reliable than guessing.
questions.explanation: The slow part is frequently not where you expect it to be.

questions.prompt: Why is this track reduced again during exam week?
options: Because split attention during an exam week hurts both
questions.explanation: The same protection as SAA week, for the same reason.

questions.prompt: Why keep doing fifteen minutes rather than stopping?
options: Because restarting a broken habit is harder than maintaining a small one
questions.explanation: The streak is the asset worth protecting.

questions.prompt: Why review rather than learn new material during exam week?
options: Because review consolidates without adding cognitive load
questions.explanation: New concepts compete for exactly the attention the exam needs.

questions.prompt: What should you do the evening before an exam?
questions.explanation: The same advice as SAA week, and it was right then too.

questions.prompt: Why write a small script immediately after the exam?
options: So the habit survives the disruption of a big event
questions.explanation: The day after a milestone is where routines usually collapse.

questions.prompt: What is a paginator loop for?
options: Collecting every page of results rather than only the first
questions.explanation: Reading only the first page is the silent bug that makes an audit tool lie.

questions.prompt: What should you check before using data from a boto3 response?
options: That the keys you need are actually present
questions.explanation: Optional fields are common, and assuming them causes a KeyError in production.

questions.prompt: Why re read your own older code?
options: Because noticing what you would now write differently measures your progress
questions.explanation: Being able to criticise your own past code is a real sign of growth.

questions.prompt: Why make only one improvement during a review day?
options: Because a large refactor during exam week is exactly the wrong use of attention
questions.explanation: Scope control is the whole point of a light week.

questions.prompt: What are the golden signals?
questions.explanation: They describe what users experience rather than what machines are doing.

questions.prompt: How should you describe your Python level after eight months of half hour days?
options: Able to write, test and package small tools that handle real data
questions.explanation: Accurate self assessment is what you can actually defend under questioning.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of trying to do both tracks at full intensity during an exam week?
options: You do both badly rather than one well
questions.explanation: This is the same reasoning that shaped Ramadan and both exam weeks.

questions.prompt: Reducing a secondary track during a high pressure week is planning rather than laziness.
questions.explanation: Every long plan that survives has this built into it deliberately.

questions.prompt: Reading your own old code is a waste of study time.
questions.explanation: It is one of the cheapest ways to see how far you have come and what to fix next.

questions.prompt: A short script on exam day is enough to keep the habit intact.
questions.explanation: Continuity matters more than volume on a disrupted day.

questions.prompt: Why emit a metric for findings split by severity?
options: Because the trend in serious findings matters more than the total count
questions.explanation: Twenty low findings and one critical are not the same situation.

questions.prompt: Why emit a metric for whether a run succeeded?
options: Because a run that never completes produces no findings and looks clean
questions.explanation: Silence and success look identical without this metric.

questions.prompt: Why alarm on run duration?
options: Because a run taking far longer than usual signals something has changed
questions.explanation: Duration is a leading indicator of problems that have not surfaced yet.

questions.prompt: Where should alarm thresholds come from?
questions.explanation: A threshold unrelated to your normal behaviour produces noise or silence.

questions.prompt: Why set retention on your log group?
options: Because storing logs forever quietly becomes a real cost
questions.explanation: It was a finding in your own audit tool, so applying it to yourself is consistent.

questions.prompt: What does Logs Insights let you do with structured logs?
questions.explanation: This is the payoff for emitting JSON rather than plain text lines.

questions.prompt: Why define log groups and alarms in Terraform?
options: So monitoring is rebuilt automatically with the environment
questions.explanation: Monitoring created by hand disappears on the next rebuild and is missed during the next incident.

questions.prompt: How do you prove monitoring is properly codified?
options: Destroy and rebuild, then confirm it came back
questions.explanation: The same destroy and rebuild proof used throughout the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What does following one correlation identifier through the logs give you?
options: The complete story of a single run
questions.explanation: It turns scattered lines into a sequence you can reason about.

questions.prompt: Why measure again after improving a slow step?
options: Because an assumed improvement is not an improvement
questions.explanation: Without the second measurement you have a belief, not a result.

questions.prompt: What makes an improvement worth putting on a CV?
options: That you can state the before and after numbers
That it used a new tool
That it took a long time
questions.explanation: A measured change is evidence, and a claimed change is an opinion.

questions.prompt: Why instrument a tool you wrote for yourself?
options: Because it runs unattended and will eventually fail quietly
questions.explanation: The scheduled audit is precisely the kind of automation nobody notices breaking.

questions.prompt: A successful run metric protects you from the failure mode where the tool stops running entirely.
questions.explanation: No findings and no runs look identical without it.

questions.prompt: Monitoring defined in the console survives a destroy and rebuild.
questions.explanation: It disappears with everything else, which is why it belongs in code.

questions.prompt: Applying your own audit findings to your own tooling is consistent rather than pedantic.
questions.explanation: A tool that flags missing log retention while having none itself is hard to defend.

questions.prompt: Why archive or delete weak repositories rather than leaving them?
options: Because a reviewer judges you by the worst thing they open
questions.explanation: Three strong repositories beat twelve where nine are abandoned exercises.

questions.prompt: Why remove commented out code before showing a repository?
options: Because it signals uncertainty and clutters the review
questions.explanation: Version control already keeps the old version, so there is no reason to keep it in the file.

questions.prompt: What should a repository README explain first?
options: What the tool does and what problem it solved
questions.explanation: A reviewer decides whether to keep reading in the first two sentences.

questions.prompt: Why include one design decision and the rejected alternative?
options: Because it shows judgement rather than just execution
questions.explanation: Interviewers ask why you chose an approach, and the README can answer it first.

questions.prompt: Why include example output in a README?
options: So a reader knows what the tool produces without running it
questions.explanation: Showing the result answers half the questions before they are asked.

questions.prompt: Why practise explaining your code out loud?
options: Because writing it and explaining it are different skills
questions.explanation: Fluency in explanation cannot be faked when you are asked to walk through your work.

questions.prompt: What kind of Python question is typical for these roles?
options: Parse a log, call an API, handle a failure
questions.explanation: Practical data and automation tasks are what infrastructure roles actually test.

questions.prompt: When would you use a set rather than a list?
options: When you need unique values or to compare two collections
questions.explanation: It is a question you will be asked, and your firewall audit is the example to give.

questions.prompt: Why practise writing scripts under a timer?
options: Because interview tasks are timed and hesitation costs you
questions.explanation: Working under mild time pressure is a separate skill from working correctly.

questions.prompt: What should you do after a timed exercise?
options: Review what slowed you down most
questions.explanation: The review is where the improvement comes from, not the attempt itself.

questions.prompt: Why record yourself explaining a project?
options: Because you cannot hear your own hesitation while speaking
questions.explanation: The recording shows what the interviewer will actually experience.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest thing your Python repositories demonstrate?
options: That you built usable tools that handle real data and real failure
questions.explanation: Usable software is a different and rarer signal than working code.

questions.prompt: A reviewer forms an impression from the worst repository they open, not the best.
questions.explanation: Which is why curating down to three strong ones is worth doing deliberately.

questions.prompt: Interview Python for infrastructure roles is usually algorithm heavy.
questions.explanation: It is normally practical: parsing, APIs, data handling and error cases.

questions.prompt: Being able to explain why you made a design choice matters as much as the choice itself.
questions.explanation: A defensible reason is what separates a decision from a coincidence.

questions.prompt: Why keep the Python part of the capstone small?
options: Because a finished small component beats an unfinished large one
questions.explanation: Scope is the usual reason a portfolio project never gets completed.

questions.prompt: Why define the interface before writing the logic?
options: Because how the rest of the system calls it constrains everything else
questions.explanation: Interfaces are expensive to change later and cheap to decide first.

questions.prompt: Why write core logic as functions that return data?
options: So it can be tested and reused rather than only printed
questions.explanation: A function that prints has already decided the output format for every caller.

questions.prompt: Why handle the three most likely failures explicitly?
options: Because those are the ones that will actually happen
questions.explanation: Exhaustive error handling is impossible, and the likely cases are where the value is.

questions.prompt: Why take configuration from the environment?
options: So the same code runs in staging and production unchanged
questions.explanation: The same principle you applied to containers and Terraform variables.

questions.prompt: Why are failure path tests more valuable than happy path tests?
options: Because the normal case usually works and the error path is untested
questions.explanation: Most real bugs live in code nobody exercises.

questions.prompt: Why make the capstone pipeline run your Python tests?
options: So a change that breaks the component is caught before it deploys
questions.explanation: A test that only runs when you remember is not a gate.

questions.prompt: Why emit a correlation identifier in the capstone component?
options: So one run can be followed through the logs during an incident
questions.explanation: You will need it on day 190 when someone breaks the system deliberately.

questions.prompt: Why trigger the capstone alarm on purpose?
options: To confirm it fires and reaches you before you need it
questions.explanation: An untested alarm has failed every time it has been counted on.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the capstone component README?
options: Purpose, install, usage, configuration and exit codes
questions.explanation: Someone should be able to run it correctly without asking you anything.

questions.prompt: Why run through your own instructions on a clean environment?
options: Because your machine has setup that your instructions do not mention
questions.explanation: It is the same works on my machine problem, applied to documentation.

questions.prompt: What has this month added to your capstone?
options: A tested, instrumented, documented component with alarms defined in code
questions.explanation: That combination is what makes it evidence of operating software rather than writing it.

questions.prompt: A component with no monitoring can still be part of a system you claim to operate.
questions.explanation: Operating means knowing when it breaks, and without monitoring you find out from a user.

questions.prompt: Testing the failure paths is where most of the real value of a test suite comes from.
questions.explanation: The happy path is exercised constantly, and the error path almost never is.

questions.prompt: Following your own README on a clean environment is a fair test of whether it is complete.
questions.explanation: If you cannot follow it, nobody else has a chance.
